title: Dye Penetrant Weld Inspection | PT of Welds (US)
description: Liquid penetrant testing of welds on stainless, aluminum and nickel alloys, root passes and repairs, mobilized across the US. Request a PT quote.
h1: Dye Penetrant Weld Inspection and Liquid Penetrant Testing of Welds
html:
Dye penetrant weld inspection finds surface-breaking cracks, lack of fusion, porosity and undercut on welds where magnetic particle testing cannot be used: stainless steel, aluminum and nickel alloys, and root passes and back-gouged joints in any material. Atlantis NDT mobilizes Level II technicians to fabrication shops, plants and construction sites across the United States. Request a PT weld inspection quote with your weld map and code.

What liquid penetrant testing of welds shows

A weld is a casting made in place, and the places where it goes wrong are mostly at the surface or just under it. Penetrant testing (PT) shows flaws that are open to the surface. A low-viscosity penetrant is applied to a clean weld, left to enter the discontinuity, and removed from the surface; a developer then draws the trapped penetrant back out, enlarging it into a visible indication. Common weld findings are:

  • Cracks: hot cracks along the centerline, crater cracks at stops, and toe cracks in heat-affected zones.
  • Lack of fusion at the sidewall or between passes, where it reaches the surface.
  • Porosity and wormholes that break the surface after grinding or cap passes.
  • Undercut, overlap and cold lap at the toes, where PT helps separate real flaws from geometry.
  • Root defects found when the root pass or back-gouged face is examined before the next pass.

It does not find flaws below the surface, tight cracks that have been closed by grinding or peening, or wall loss. When a weld needs volumetric information, the sibling method is ultrasonic testing, and for ferromagnetic welds magnetic particle inspection compared with penetrant explains why MT is often faster on carbon steel.

When PT is the right weld method

Weld situations and the usual choice
Weld situationUsual surface methodNote
Austenitic stainless or nickel alloy weldPenetrantNot ferromagnetic, so MT cannot be used
Aluminum structural or process weldPenetrantNon-magnetic; low-contamination materials are normally specified
Carbon steel fillet or groove weldMT first, PT where specifiedMT is quicker; PT if the code or the design asks for it
Root pass or back-gouged face before the next passPenetrantGives access to the surface while the joint is open
Thick weld with an internal concernUltrasonicPT only sees the surface

Codes behind a weld PT job

The examination method comes from one document and the acceptance criteria from another. ASME Section V Article 6 and ASTM E165 describe how penetrant examination is done in the field, and ASTM E1417 covers fluorescent process control. The construction code sets what is rejectable: ASME B31.3 for process piping, with liquid penetrant examination described in paragraph 344.4; ASME Section VIII for pressure vessels; AWS D1.1 for structural steel, where the inspection clause governs; and API 1104 for pipeline welds. Where a contract names none, we ask your engineer which one applies before we write the procedure. Written procedures are approved by an ASNT Level III, and technicians are qualified to the company written practice under SNT-TC-1A.

For the overall weld inspection program, including visual and ultrasonic examination on the same joints, see our weld inspection page.

Technique, step by step

  1. Prepare the weld. Remove slag, spatter and scale. Grinding or wire brushing can smear metal over a flaw, so surface preparation is specified in the procedure and avoids blasting before PT. If the weld was ground, lightly etch where the procedure requires it.
  2. Check temperature. The standard range in Article 6 is 40 to 125 °F (5 to 52 °C). Outside it, the procedure must be qualified at the actual temperature by using a comparator block, a step we record in the report. Hot welds just after post-weld heat treatment are a common problem and should cool first.
  3. Apply penetrant. Visible solvent-removable dye is the field default; fluorescent is used where the specification demands higher sensitivity and a darkened area is available.
  4. Dwell. Dwell time is taken from the procedure and the material and flaw type. Longer dwell helps on tight cracks; too long lets penetrant dry on the surface.
  5. Remove excess. Wipe with lint-free cloth moistened with solvent. Do not flood-wash or spray on the weld, which can pull penetrant out of flaws.
  6. Apply developer. A thin, even coat of non-aqueous developer. A thick coat hides small indications.
  7. Interpret. Look at the weld after the developing time and again as indications bleed out. Rate bleed-out as relevant or non-relevant and record the size.
  8. Post-clean. Remove developer and penetrant residue, especially before painting, coating or further welding.

Interpreting weld indications

Experience matters most at this step. Round indications with slow, steady bleed-out are usually porosity. A continuous line is a crack or a lack of fusion. Weld ripples, spatter, arc strikes and rough toes produce non-relevant or false indications that need to be re-wiped and re-tested rather than argued about. Indications are measured at the largest dimension, classified by shape, and judged against the acceptance criteria in the code. When an indication is rejected, the repair is by grinding or excavation, welding and a repeat of the full penetrant process on the repaired area.

Materials and special cases

On austenitic stainless and nickel-base welds, ASME Section V limits the sulfur and halogen content of penetrant materials. The stainless steel penetrant page explains the contaminant limits in detail. For hygienic equipment, the food and pharma penetrant page covers the post-cleaning that equipment needs. In chemical plants and on chemical process equipment we adjust the plan to the service fluid. For cryogenic and gas plants, see LNG equipment penetrant testing, and for structural shop work, fabrication shop penetrant testing shows how we examine weldments before shipment. Aluminum welds in aviation tooling and support equipment follow the customer's specification; Atlantis does not sign off airworthiness.

Weld types and what we look for

Different processes leave different signatures. Gas tungsten arc root passes on stainless pipe can show lack of fusion and oxidized roots when the back purge was poor. Shielded metal arc and flux-cored welds can carry slag lines and toe undercut that PT helps separate from real cracks. Aluminum welds are prone to porosity and, in the heat-affected zone, liquation cracking. Nickel-base overlays and dissimilar-metal joints crack at fusion boundaries. Fillet welds on lugs and supports show toe cracks first. The technician reads the weld with the process and the material in mind, so a line on a fillet toe is treated differently from the same line at a crater.

Visible dye or fluorescent

Visible solvent-removable dye is portable, needs no darkened area and works in most field conditions, which makes it the default on site. Fluorescent systems use ultraviolet light in a darkened area and reveal finer indications, so specifications for critical parts often require them, and they suit shop and bench work better than outdoor joints. The procedure states which is used. If you are not sure, tell us the component and the code and we will propose one.

Planning realities for weld PT

Technicians are mobilized to your site for an agreed scope. Penetrant testing is wet and needs a reasonably clean, dry weld, adequate light and ventilation, so the weld should be accessible before insulation, coating or paint goes on. Outdoors, wind, rain and cold affect the technique and the temperature range; welds in shade or under a tent are easier to examine. Inside vessels and tanks, confined space rules apply and solvents need ventilation. Typical plant requirements such as hot-work permits, lockout and site orientation are arranged ahead of time.

Repairs and re-examination

When an indication is rejected, the excavation is blended and checked with penetrant before welding so the original flaw is gone, then the new weld is examined again after it cools. Repeated repairs on the same joint are tracked in the report, because most codes limit the number of repair attempts or call for added examination after a second repair. We list each cycle so your engineer sees the full history of the joint rather than only the final pass.

What the report contains

Every weld PT report lists the project, weld or joint identification, the weld map reference, material and thickness, the procedure and revision, penetrant system with lot numbers and contaminant certification where required, surface and ambient temperature, dwell and developer times, technician and level, indications sketched with location and length, and accept or reject against the named code. Photos of indications are attached when you want them. An ASNT Level III reviews the report. We do not calculate remaining life or approve repairs.

What to send for a quote

  • Weld maps or drawings with the joints to be examined.
  • Material, thickness, process and heat treatment.
  • Governing code, edition and acceptance criteria.
  • Surface condition and whether welds are as-welded or ground.
  • Expected temperatures and whether the work is indoors or outdoors.
  • Access, lighting, power, permits, badging and the site address.

Where we work in the United States

  • Houston for pressure vessels, piping and fabrication around the Ship Channel.
  • Baton Rouge for chemical and refining welds along the Mississippi River corridor.
  • Chicago for steel fabrication and boiler work across the upper Midwest.
  • Philadelphia for process piping in pharmaceutical and chemical plants.
  • Newark for refinery and chemical piping in northern New Jersey.
  • Seattle for aluminum and stainless fabrication and marine weldments in the Pacific Northwest.
  • Indianapolis for fabricators and process plants in Indiana.
  • Cleveland for steel, castings and machine welds in northern Ohio.

Train your own technicians

If your shop wants its own PT capability, PT Level 1 and PT Level 2 training cover the method, supported by the penetrant testing simulator and a plain explanation of Article 6. Under SNT-TC-1A your employer certifies its own technicians.

What we do not do

Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States, and we do not offer specialist techniques on this page. We do not choose weld acceptance criteria or approve repairs; your engineer or the owner's authorized inspector does that.

faq.q: Why use dye penetrant instead of magnetic particle on a weld?
faq.a: Magnetic particle testing only works on ferromagnetic materials. Austenitic stainless, aluminum and nickel alloys are not magnetic, so penetrant is the surface method there. It is also used on root passes and any weld where the code or contract specifies penetrant.

faq.q: What temperature range can PT be done at?
faq.a: ASME Section V Article 6 gives a standard range of 40 to 125 °F, or 5 to 52 °C. Outside that range the procedure must be qualified at the actual temperature using a comparator block. Hot welds should cool first, because penetrant dries and loses sensitivity on warm surfaces.

faq.q: How long must penetrant dwell on a weld?
faq.a: Dwell time comes from the approved procedure and depends on the material, the type of flaw and the temperature. Tight cracks need longer dwell than porosity. We follow the procedure and the penetrant manufacturer's range and record the actual times in the report.

faq.q: Can you test welds right after grinding?
faq.a: Grinding can smear metal across the opening of a flaw and hide it. The procedure may call for a light etch or a defined waiting period first, and blasting is avoided before PT. We agree the surface preparation with your engineer before the examination.

faq.q: What codes apply to weld PT in the United States?
faq.a: Method rules come from ASME Section V Article 6 and ASTM E165; acceptance comes from the construction code, for example ASME B31.3 for piping, ASME Section VIII for vessels, AWS D1.1 for structural steel or API 1104 for pipelines. Your engineer names the one for the job.

faq.q: What does a rejectable weld indication mean for the repair?
faq.a: The flaw is removed by grinding or excavation, the area is re-welded, and the repaired area is re-examined with the full penetrant process. The code and your authorized inspector decide whether the repair needs additional examination. We report the result.

faq.q: Can you do PT on a weld that is already painted?
faq.a: Coatings must be removed from the weld and a margin around it so penetrant can reach the metal, because a coating can bridge a flaw. We agree the stripping method with your engineer and avoid abrasive methods that close cracks.

A Level II technician qualified under the company written practice performs and interprets the examination, and an ASNT Level III approves the procedure and reviews the report. The code you name decides acceptance, and your engineer or inspector applies it.

faq.q: What do you need to quote a weld PT job?
faq.a: A weld map or drawing, material and thickness, governing code and edition, surface condition, expected temperatures, access and lighting, permits, and the site address. If you also need ultrasonic or visual examination on the same welds, tell us and we scope them together.
